ethiopia.content: ENDC–IFA Policy Dialogue Concludes with a Focus on Ethiopia’s National Security and Strategic Interests - IFA Contact Us English Subscribe Topics Regions Events Publications Academy Media About Us ← Back to Blog News • 2 min read • October 22, 2026 ENDC–IFA Policy Dialogue Concludes with a Focus on Ethiopia’s National Security and Strategic Interests ENDC–IFA Policy Dialogue Concludes with a Focus on Ethiopia’s National Security and Strategic Interests ENDC–IFA Policy Dialogue Concludes with a Focus on Ethiopia’s National Security and Strategic Interests The Ethiopian National Defence College (ENDC), in collaboration with the Institute of Foreign Affairs (IFA), concluded a policy dialogue titled “Unity or Betrayal? Where Is the Anti-Ethiopia Coalition Headed?” The dialogue brought together policymakers, security experts, and researchers to examine emerging regional security challenges and their implications for Ethiopia’s national interests. The discussions explored evolving political alliances, insurgent movements, and geopolitical developments in the Horn of Africa, with particular attention to Ethiopia–Eritrea relations. Speakers examined the strategic motivations behind regional alliances, the potential implications of external involvement in internal security challenges, and the importance of understanding shifting regional power dynamics. Participants emphasized the need to safeguard Ethiopia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national security through stronger institutions, enhanced defense capabilities, and coordinated policy responses. The dialogue also highlighted the importance of national unity, internal stability, and peaceful conflict resolution in reducing vulnerabilities to external pressures. The discussions further underscored the role of proactive diplomacy, regional cooperation, and sustained engagement with neighboring countries. Particular attention was given to Ethiopia’s maritime access interests, the strategic significance of the Red Sea, and the importance of pursuing mutually beneficial arrangements consistent with international law. The dialogue concluded by emphasizing the importance of translating strategic assessments into coordinated diplomatic and institutional action. It reaffirmed the value of continued policy dialogue, research, and cooperation in advancing Ethiopia’s long-term national interests while contributing to peace and stability in the Horn of Africa. #IFAEthiopia #ENDC #Ethiopia #NationalSecurity #Diplomacy #HornOfAfrica # Regions Horn of Africa (Ethiopia, Somalia, Somaliland, Eritrea, Djibouti) Category News Share this article 𝕏 Twitter f Facebook in LinkedIn Institute of Foreign Affairs (IFA) bridges research, policy, and action for sustainable global development. Where Is the Anti-Ethiopia Coalition Headed?” This event gathered policymakers, security experts, and researchers to discuss the emerging security challenges in the Horn of Africa and their implications for Ethiopia's national interests. Key topics included evolving political alliances, insurgent movements, and the geopolitical landscape, particularly concerning Ethiopia–Eritrea relations. Participants emphasized the necessity of safeguarding Ethiopia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity through enhanced defense capabilities and coordinated policy responses. The dialogue highlighted the importance of national unity, internal stability, and peaceful conflict resolution to mitigate vulnerabilities to external pressures. Additionally, it underscored the significance of proactive diplomacy and regional cooperation, particularly regarding Ethiopia's maritime access and the strategic importance of the Red Sea. The discussions concluded with a call for translating strategic assessments into actionable diplomatic and institutional efforts to promote Ethiopia's long-term interests and regional stability.

ethiopia.title: Eritrea’s Antagonistic Policy Threatens Regional Stability, Says Prof. Alemayehu - ENA English
ethiopia.content: Eritrea’s Antagonistic Policy Threatens Regional Stability, Says Prof. Alemayehu - ENA English - ENA Skip to Content Eritrea’s Antagonistic Policy Threatens Regional Stability, Says Prof. Alemayehu - ENA English Live: አማርኛ ትግርኛ Afaan Oromoo Af‑Soomaali Qafar Afa English Français عربي Politics Social Economy Sport Technology Environment Feature Videos About Us Eritrea’s Antagonistic Policy Threatens Regional Stability, Says Prof. Alemayehu 🔇Unmute Addis Ababa, October 22, 2026 (ENA) — Eritrea’s confrontational approach toward Ethiopia threatens regional security and undermines prospects for peace, economic cooperation and integration across the Horn of Africa, Ethiopian American scholar Emeritus Professor Alemayehu G. Mariam underscored. the former California State University, San Bernardino professor said Eritrea’s leadership viewed Ethiopia as a strategic adversary and considered instability in its larger neighbor advantageous to the survival of its own government. “Since they cannot militarily overcome Ethiopia, their best approach is to destabilize Ethiopia every way they can,” he told POA, describing what he characterized as Asmara’s strategy toward Addis Ababa. Professor Alemayehu further elaborated that Eritrea’s leadership viewed Ethiopia’s internal divisions and conflicts as serving its own political interests. He said the Shabia regime believes that the more unstable, divided, and conflict-ridden Ethiopia becomes, the stronger the Eritrean government becomes. He added Eritrea is supporting armed groups hostile to the Ethiopian state, supplying weapons and military equipment, and facilitating military assistance from Egypt and Sudan. He said, this reflected a broader strategy of weakening Ethiopia rather than pursuing constructive bilateral relations. Contrasting the two countries’ approaches, Alemayehu said Ethiopia was pursuing regional economic integration, expanded markets and shared prosperity, while Eritrea’s confrontational posture was obstructing opportunities for cooperation and development across the Horn of Africa. He also criticized Eritrea’s domestic political system, describing it as authoritarian and focused on preserving the ruling government’s hold on power. The absence of elected national leadership, political repression and the continued exodus of young people, he argued, had imposed significant costs on Eritrean society and contributed to regional instability. On security, Professor Alemayehu said Eritrean troops had entered Ethiopian territory, citing satellite imagery and ground-level video recordings as evidence. He argued that international calls for Eritrea to respect Ethiopia’s sovereignty had not adequately addressed the issue. He called for a firm response from Ethiopia as continued military incursions and support for armed groups operating against Ethiopia. Alemayehu also characterized the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) as a proxy through which Eritrea had sought to exert pressure on Ethiopia. He argued that the weakening of the group had constrained Asmara’s ability to destabilize its neighbor. “If Eritrea continues its military incursions into Ethiopia, Ethiopia will have the right of self-defense,” he said. He further argued that such a response could include what he termed anticipatory self-defense and the possible establishment of a security or buffer zone inside Eritrea to prevent further cross-border attacks. On Eritrea’s political future, Professor Alemayehu said change could emerge from within the country or through external pressure. He maintained that continued confrontation with Ethiopia would remain an obstacle to lasting peace and regional cooperation. © Ethiopian News Agency 2023 Hidden

He argues that Eritrea's leadership perceives Ethiopia as a strategic adversary, believing that fostering instability in Ethiopia benefits its own regime's survival. ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed Honours Kenya's National Heroes - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's Abiy Ahmed Honours Kenya's National Heroes 21 October 2026 Horn Diplomat (Hargeisa) By Kadir Moustapha Nairobi, Kenya — Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed paid tribute to Kenya's freedom fighters and national heroes during Mashujaa Day celebrations in Eldoret on Tuesday, highlighting the two countries' shared history of struggle, sacrifice and national unity. Speaking at the celebrations on October 20, Abiy praised the courage of Kenyans who fought for independence and those who sacrificed their lives to defend their country. The Ethiopian leader drew parallels between Kenya's struggle for freedom and Ethiopia's historic Battle of Adwa, when Ethiopian forces defeated an invading Italian army in 1896. "Kenya's history of courage and sacrifice resonates deeply with Ethiopia's own story of Adwa, where Ethiopians from every corner of the country united to defend their homeland," Abiy said in a statement posted on X. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines "These shared histories remind us that freedom was never given; it was won through courage, unity, and sacrifice." Abiy also called for stronger economic cooperation between Ethiopia and Kenya, identifying clean energy, regional connectivity, telecommunications and trade as key areas for expanding bilateral relations. "As our histories are intertwined, so too must our futures be," he said. "Through the spirit of Medemer, Ethiopia and Kenya must continue building on our existing cooperation in clean energy, connectivity, telecommunications, and trade to create greater opportunities and shared prosperity for our people." Medemer, a concept promoted by Abiy, emphasises unity, cooperation and collective efforts towards national development. Ethiopia and Kenya maintain close diplomatic and economic relations, with cooperation covering infrastructure development, electricity trade, regional security and cross-border connectivity. The two East African neighbours have also worked to strengthen regional economic integration through transport and energy infrastructure projects aimed at improving trade and investment opportunities. Mashujaa Day, celebrated annually on October 20, honours Kenyans who contributed to the country's independence and national development. Abiy concluded his remarks by saluting those recognised during the celebrations. "To all those honoured today, I salute you. Happy Mashujaa Day!" he said. Read the original article on Horn Diplomat . ethiopia.title: Who Protects the Protectors? Inside the Growing Danger for Ethiopia's Humanitarian Workers
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Who Protects the Protectors? Inside the Growing Danger for Ethiopia's Humanitarian Workers - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Who Protects the Protectors? Inside the Growing Danger for Ethiopia's Humanitarian Workers 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — When humanitarian workers travel to the field, they carry more than food, medicine, or information. They carry the hopes of people facing hunger, displacement, illness, and conflict. Yet, the danger increasingly exposes those delivering this assistance. In Ethiopia, humanitarian workers have been killed, kidnapped, threatened, robbed, and caught in crossfire. Some have been abducted for ransom. Others have lost their lives while carrying out routine duties. These are not simply workplace accidents or unfortunate incidents. They raise serious questions about the protection of people who help others survive crises. The question is simple: Who protects the people who protect others? Ethiopia needs to move beyond telling aid workers to be careful. It needs a system that prevents avoidable harm, supports those affected, investigates serious incidents, and ensures that national and local responders are not left to carry the risks alone. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn From kidnappings to drone strikes Consider the death of Mahelet Sitotaw Abera, a staff member of ORDA Ethiopia. On 20 June 2025, she was collecting humanitarian data in Angot District, North Wollo, when she was critically wounded during crossfire between government forces and non-state armed groups. She died later that day. The United Nations condemned her death and called for the protection of humanitarian personnel. In 2024, Ethiopian NGO worker Yared Melese was abducted in North Wollo. His kidnappers demanded a ransom. His death was confirmed in August, according to The New Humanitarian's investigation . The danger is not limited to national organizations. On 24 June 2021, three Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) staff members --María Hernández Matas, Tedros Gebremariam Gebremichael, and Yohannes Halefom Reda--were killed in Tigray. In June 2026, MSF said the families had still not received the findings of a credible and impartial investigation. MSF's internal review had concluded that the clearly identified humanitarian workers were deliberately targeted. These incidents are different. Mahelet died during crossfire, Yared was abducted, and MSF maintains that its colleagues were deliberately targeted. They should not be treated as legally identical. But each raises urgent questions about prevention, protection, and accountability. No one should have to risk their life simply to help others survive." The wider situation remains concerning. On 30 September 2026, the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Ethiopia reported that at least ten humanitarian vehicles had been seized by armed groups between 2025 and 2026, with only two recovered at the time of the statement. The UN also expressed concern about incidents affecting aid personnel, humanitarian assets, and premises. The global picture is equally troubling. According to the Aid Worker Security Database , 713 major incidents affecting aid workers were recorded in 2025, compared with 637 in 2024. A Reuters report published in August 2026 said that 907 aid workers were killed, injured, or kidnapped in 2025. These figures measure different aspects of violence and should not be confused: one counts recorded incidents, while the other counts people affected. On World Humanitarian Day, 19 August 2026 , the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that armed drones were changing the risks faced by humanitarian workers. OCHA reported that 350 aid workers were killed, 322 injured, and 235 kidnapped worldwide in 2025. It also reported that, during the first part of 2026, a further 82 aid workers had been killed, 97 injured, and 39 kidnapped. The message was clear: public condemnation alone is not enough. States and parties to armed conflict must respect international humanitarian law and ensure accountability for violations. This threat has also become a direct concern in Ethiopia. On 20 September 2026, a humanitarian truck carrying approximately 41 tonnes of food assistance for internally displaced people in Sheraro, northwestern Tigray, was reportedly hit during drone strikes while travelling along a road in the region. Addis Standard reported the incident. The truck was transporting food intended for displaced families who depend on humanitarian assistance. Reports differed on the driver's injuries and how much of the cargo was lost, so those details should be treated cautiously. The attack drew international concern. Human Rights Watch reported that the United States condemned the strike on the humanitarian convoy. The incident is a serious warning: when humanitarian transport is hit, the danger extends beyond the driver and the vehicle. Food supplies may be lost, deliveries delayed, and already vulnerable families left waiting for assistance. The available reports establish that the convoy was struck, but responsibility for the attack should not be asserted without reliable evidence. The use of armed drones raises difficult questions for humanitarian protection. A vehicle carrying relief supplies may be exposed to attack even when it is travelling to support civilians. Humanitarian organizations must continually reassess security risks, protect staff and drivers, review routes and movement procedures, and ensure that personnel can stop a journey when conditions become unacceptable. But these measures cannot replace the responsibility of parties to a conflict to respect humanitarian personnel and relief operations under applicable international law. Behind every statistic is a person, a family, and a community that may lose access to essential assistance. Ethiopia needs credible investigations into serious incidents, public accountability where appropriate, and practical measures to prevent attacks from happening again. My Own Experience: Danger does not end when an incident is over My concern about aid-worker safety comes not only from reports and statistics but also from what I personally experienced while travelling through a conflict-affected area. On one occasion, armed men wearing military-style uniforms stopped several vehicles along the road. At first, we assumed they were government security personnel conducting a routine checkpoint inspection. We soon realized they were members of a non-state armed group impersonating security personnel. They ordered all passengers to get off the vehicles and lie face-down in muddy water beside the road. We were forced to remain there, unable to raise our heads, fearing for our lives. When a woman and two male passengers objected to the order, one of the armed men shot them. All three died in front of us. The armed men then took passengers' mobile phones, money, jewelry, watches, and other valuables. Several vehicles, including other buses, were looted. When we were finally released, I discovered that I had lost my laptop, camera, tablet, clothing, and other belongings. More painfully, I lost months of humanitarian assessment data, photographs, field documentation, and research materials. Their loss disrupted my work and meant that valuable information gathered in the field could no longer be used without significant effort to recover or reconstruct it. The effects went beyond material loss. I had witnessed three people being killed and feared for my own life. The experience reminded me that surviving a security incident does not mean its consequences end when the immediate danger passes. I share this experience because incident reports cannot fully capture the human cost of insecurity. Behind the statistics are people whose lives, families, work, and sense of safety are changed forever. When aid workers are attacked or robbed, humanitarian operations and the communities depending on them can also suffer. This must lead to action. Governments and parties to armed conflict must respect humanitarian personnel and their work. Humanitarian organizations and donors must provide realistic resources for staff protection, emergency support, and care for survivors and families. Serious incidents must be investigated, and those responsible must be held accountable where the evidence supports it. Protecting aid workers is not simply about protecting organizations or projects. It is about preserving the lifeline between people in crisis and the assistance they need. No one should have to risk their life simply to help others survive. Why do aid workers remain at risk? There is no single explanation. In conflict areas, humanitarian workers may be caught in fighting, deliberately attacked, kidnapped for ransom, or threatened because their work is misunderstood or politicized. Vehicles, supplies, and equipment may also be seized. Elsewhere, risks may arise from crime, extortion, administrative restrictions, community disputes, misinformation, or pressure from powerful local actors. The danger is not only about the threats workers face. It is also about how organizations prepare for them. Three factors help explain why the same environment can be more dangerous for some workers than for others. First, "threat" refers to the possibility of harm, such as armed violence, kidnapping, or detention. Second, exposure concerns how often and in what circumstances workers encounter that threat. Third, vulnerability describes the factors that make harm more likely or make it harder to prevent and respond to an incident. These are common elements of humanitarian security risk management. The Global Interagency Security Forum's Security to Go toolkit explains how aid organizations can assess risks and strengthen their security arrangements. For example, two organizations may operate in the same district, but one may have reliable communications, updated security information, and emergency medical arrangements, while the other lacks these resources. Their workers may face similar threats but have very different levels of protection. Research and humanitarian security guidance also point to an important responsibility: organizations must consider the risks faced by different groups of workers, including national staff. The Global Interagency Security Forum's guidance on managing the security of aid workers with diverse profiles highlights the relationship between a worker's circumstances, their role, and their organization's responsibility to take reasonable steps to protect them. A staff member may understand the risks and still feel unable to refuse a journey because a deadline is approaching, funding is limited, or a manager expects the activity to proceed. This is why security cannot depend only on an individual worker's judgment or courage. A credible protection system must allow workers to raise concerns, delay travel, and stop an activity when the risks become unacceptable. Managers must take these concerns seriously, and workers must not be unfairly penalized for refusing an unsafe assignment. This responsibility is also reflected in United Nations Security Council Resolution 2730 (2024) , which calls on states and parties to armed conflict to respect and protect humanitarian personnel and comply with applicable international humanitarian law. Protecting aid workers requires both respect for these legal obligations and practical action by humanitarian organizations to reduce foreseeable risks. Localization Without Resources: Shifting risk, not power National and local organizations are often close to the communities they serve. Their staff speak local languages, understand social relationships, and can reach people whom others may struggle to reach. Their knowledge is an important humanitarian asset. But local knowledge does not make local responders invulnerable. Localization must not mean that local people carry the risk alone." National staffs continue living in conflict-affected areas when international colleagues relocate. Local NGOs are expected to maintain assistance in dangerous locations while decisions about budgets, program deadlines and security arrangements are made elsewhere. Community volunteers, local health workers and informal responders face even greater challenges. They can be the first to respond to an emergency, yet have limited security training, insurance, emergency assistance or formal recognition. This does not mean that all international organizations provide adequate protection or that every national NGO lacks it. The issue is whether protection reflects the risks people actually face, rather than their job title, nationality or employer. Global funding evidence makes this concern difficult to ignore. A May 2026 study by ODI found that just below 10% of international humanitarian funding reached local and national actors directly and indirectly in 2024. Only 3.8% reached them directly. The report also found that local actors often receive shorter, smaller, and more restricted grants than international counterparts. These are global figures, not Ethiopia-specific estimates, but they illustrate the wider financing problem. When local organizations have limited funding for insurance, security management, emergency medical care and staff support, they struggle to protect the people expected to deliver assistance. This is the localization paradox: local actors are encouraged to lead, but the money, authority and protection needed to lead safely may remain elsewhere. As I argued in my earlier Addis Standard article , transferring responsibility to local organizations is not enough if resources and decision-making power do not follow. Localization must not mean transferring risk to local organizations while keeping control and protection resources elsewhere. Public Trust, Community Acceptance: Important, but insufficient substitutes for protection Humanitarian security often relies on three approaches: acceptance, protection, and deterrence. The Global Interagency Security Forum (GISF) identifies these as complementary elements of humanitarian security risk management. Acceptance means building trust with communities and relevant local actors. Organizations explain who they are, why they are present, how assistance is selected, and how people can raise complaints. They listen to concerns and correct mistakes. Protection involves practical measures such as risk assessments, safe travel arrangements, reliable communications, staff training, and emergency plans. Deterrence aims to discourage attacks through appropriate engagement, legal consequences, and action by responsible authorities. These approaches must work together. Community trust cannot replace practical safety measures, and neither can replace accountability. As GISF's guidance on community acceptance explains, acceptance requires sustained relationship-building and cannot be taken for granted. In Ethiopia, elders, religious leaders, women's groups, youth representatives, customary institutions, and local volunteers may help identify tensions, correct misinformation, and resolve disputes before they escalate. When people believe assistance is being distributed unfairly, for example, clear eligibility criteria and accessible complaints processes can help address concerns before they threaten staff safety. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) highlights the value of listening to communities, sharing information, and creating opportunities for feedback. Customary institutions, including the Gadaa system among Oromo communities , also offer lessons in mediation and collective responsibility. Their role must be understood in its specific context. Such institutions can contribute to trust, but they cannot guarantee safety or replace formal legal protection. Acceptance is not equal for everyone. Shared language, religion, ethnicity, or local identity may help some workers build relationships, while others may face suspicion or discrimination. Women may also experience gender-based harassment and other risks linked to how they are perceived. Two workers performing the same task may therefore experience different levels of safety. Organizations must recognize these differences without stereotyping communities or expecting local leaders to put themselves at risk to protect aid workers. Public perceptions also matter. People may question why some households receive assistance while others do not. Rumors, political accusations, and online misinformation can deepen suspicion and, in some circumstances, contribute to threats against humanitarian personnel. Humanitarian Outcomes' Aid Worker Security Report 2025 examines the changing security environment for aid workers, including concerns about declining acceptance and hostile narratives. The ICRC's guidance on harmful information explains how false or misleading information can undermine trust and put humanitarian workers and affected communities at risk. Humanitarian organizations must respond through transparency, accountability, and effective communication. They should explain assistance criteria, listen to complaints, and address legitimate criticism rather than dismiss it. Community radio, local-language discussions, schools, religious leaders, and trusted digital communicators can help explain humanitarian principles and why attacks on aid workers disrupt essential services. Trusted local content producers could help deliver accurate, accessible messages to wider audiences. However, campaigns must avoid political propaganda, protect sensitive information, and ensure that sharing stories or images does not expose staff or communities to further danger. The aim is to encourage informed public discussion, not to silence criticism or portray every critical voice as hostile. Awareness must also reach relevant government institutions, military personnel, and armed actors. Under applicable international humanitarian law, humanitarian relief personnel are entitled to protection in the circumstances set out in the relevant rules. Article 71 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions addresses personnel participating in relief actions, while Rule 31 of the ICRC's Customary IHL Study sets out the customary rule on the protection of humanitarian relief personnel. Public awareness alone is not enough. Training, engagement with authorities and military command structures, credible investigations, and accountability for violations must reinforce these legal obligations. Ultimately, communities can help create a safer environment, and responsible communication can strengthen trust. But humanitarian workers must not be left to depend on goodwill alone. Community acceptance is one part of protection; the responsibility to respect applicable law, protect humanitarian personnel, and hold perpetrators accountable remains essential. From legal promise to practical reality International humanitarian law provides important protection for humanitarian relief personnel during armed conflict, subject to the applicable legal rules. The International Committee of the Red Cross identifies the protection of humanitarian relief personnel in customary international humanitarian law. In May 2024, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2730, calling on states and parties to armed conflict to respect and protect humanitarian personnel and to address impunity for violations. These protections are not favors. They reflect legal obligations. However, having laws is not the same as enforcing them. Serious incidents must be documented and investigated through appropriate channels. Recent incidents highlight the urgent need for better protection systems for these workers. For instance, Mahelet Sitotaw Abera was fatally injured in crossfire while collecting humanitarian data, and Yared Melese was abducted for ransom, later confirmed dead. The UN has condemned these attacks, emphasizing the necessity for accountability and protection under international humanitarian law. The situation is exacerbated by armed groups seizing humanitarian vehicles and the use of drones, which pose new risks to aid operations. Reports indicate a significant increase in violence against aid workers globally, with hundreds affected in 2025 alone. The article stresses that protecting humanitarian personnel is crucial not only for their safety but also for the communities relying on their assistance. Effective measures must be implemented to ensure their safety and uphold their vital role in crisis response.

ethiopia.title: Obituary - Prominent Kenyan Oromo Scholar, Anthropologist Professor Abdullahi Shongolo Passes Away
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Obituary - Prominent Kenyan Oromo Scholar, Anthropologist Professor Abdullahi Shongolo Passes Away - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Obituary - Prominent Kenyan Oromo Scholar, Anthropologist Professor Abdullahi Shongolo Passes Away 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Professor Abdullahi Shongolo, a prominent scholar of history and anthropology whose research on Borana Oromo culture, customary law, and history brought international attention to the community's rich heritage, passed away on 20 October at the age of 68 at Nanyuki Hospital in Kenya, following an illness from which he did not recover. Born in 1958 in Moyale, Kenya, Professor Shongolo completed his education in Kenya. He worked in various parts of the country and served in Kenya's Ministry of Education, rising to the position of Assistant Director of Education. Jaatani Diidaa, a cultural and historical researcher, told Addis Standard that Professor Shongolo devoted much of his life to in-depth research, making significant personal sacrifices to bring the educational and cultural heritage of the Oromo of Kenya and Ethiopia to international attention. Professor Shongolo made substantial contributions to anthropological research, serving as a senior researcher at Germany's renowned Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology for more than two decades, from 1999 to 2019, according to Jaatani. During the 2000s, he also served as an Associate Research Fellow in the Department of Social Anthropology at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden, where he pursued research and academic work. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Among his major scholarly contributions were books co-authored with prominent German scholar Professor Günther Schlee, including Pastoralism and Politics in Northern Kenya and Southern Ethiopia and Islam and Ethnicity in Northern Kenya and Southern Ethiopia . He also documented traditional Borana oral literature and proverbs in Boran Proverbs in Their Cultural Context . These works helped bring greater international recognition to Oromo history, pastoral life, religious traditions, and customary systems of governance, particularly the Oromo customary governance, Gumii Gaayo Assembly. Professor Shongolo's passing "has brought profound grief and shock to the Borana Oromo community, the wider Oromo community across the world, and people in Kenya and Ethiopia, as well as to scholars in the international academic community, Jaatani said. ethiopia.summary: Professor Abdullahi Shongolo, a distinguished Kenyan Oromo scholar and anthropologist, passed away on October 20, 2026, at the age of 68 in Nanyuki Hospital, Kenya, after a prolonged illness. Born in 1958 in Moyale, he dedicated his life to the study of Borana Oromo culture, history, and customary law, significantly enhancing the community's global recognition. Shongolo's academic journey included roles in Kenya's Ministry of Education, where he became Assistant Director, and extensive research at Germany's Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology from 1999 to 2019. He also contributed to the University of Gothenburg in Sweden as an Associate Research Fellow. His notable works, including collaborations with Professor Günther Schlee, explored themes of pastoralism, politics, and the cultural context of Borana proverbs. His death has deeply affected the Borana Oromo community and the broader Oromo population, as well as scholars worldwide. His funeral took place on October 21 in Nanyuki, marking a significant loss for many.

ethiopia.title: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Ethiopia's rule of law performance has deteriorated further, with the country ranking 133rd out of 143 countries and jurisdictions in the 2026 World Justice Project (WJP) Rule of Law Index, according to the ranking provided for this report. The latest assessment extends a multi-year decline that has seen the country remain near the bottom of global and sub-Saharan African comparisons. The 2026 index, released on 21 October, comes as the WJP warns that authoritarian practices are becoming entrenched worldwide, with weakened checks on executive power, declining judicial independence and restrictions on fundamental freedoms contributing to a prolonged global deterioration in the rule of law. The WJP said the global rule-of-law recession had continued for a ninth consecutive year, with 62% of the countries and jurisdictions assessed recording declines, compared with 38% that improved. Although the share of countries experiencing deterioration fell from 68% in 2025, the overall direction remained negative. The latest findings reinforce concerns about institutional accountability and civic freedoms in Ethiopia, where successive editions of the index have documented persistent weaknesses in constraints on government authority, fundamental rights, open government and the enforcement of regulations. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn A sustained decline across successive editions Ethiopia's latest ranking follows a pattern documented by Addis Standard in previous years. In the 2025 edition, the country ranked 132nd out of 143 countries, with its overall score falling by 2.4% from the previous year to 0.36. It placed 30th among 34 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, highlighting the depth of its institutional weaknesses relative to regional peers. The decline has persisted across multiple editions. Ethiopia ranked 129th out of 142 countries in 2023, with a score of 0.38, after placing 123rd out of 140 countries in 2022. In the 2024 edition, it ranked 130th out of 142 countries, recording a further 2.4% fall in its overall score. The successive declines point to a longer-term deterioration rather than a one-year fluctuation. They also come against a backdrop of armed conflicts, restrictions on civic freedoms and concerns over the independence and effectiveness of public institutions. Checks on government power, fundamental rights remain weak The 2025 index offers a detailed picture of the areas contributing to Ethiopia's poor performance. The country ranked 134th globally for constraints on government powers, 138th for fundamental rights, 135th for open government and 137th for regulatory enforcement. Its rankings were somewhat higher in civil justice, at 124th, and criminal justice, at 104th. It ranked 96th for absence of corruption. The figures suggest that the weakest areas extend beyond the operation of courts. They include the mechanisms through which government decisions are scrutinized, public institutions are held accountable and citizens exercise fundamental freedoms. The WJP's constraints-on-government-powers measure assesses whether those exercising public authority are bound by law and subject to institutional and non-governmental checks. These include legislative oversight, judicial limits on executive authority and the role of an independent press in holding government to account. Ethiopia's low ranking in this category is particularly significant given longstanding concerns about the relationship between political authority and independent institutions. The country's scores in open government and fundamental rights also point to persistent challenges involving access to information, civic participation and freedoms of expression, assembly and association. The index does not, by itself, establish the cause of every institutional weakness or determine responsibility for individual violations. It provides a comparative assessment based on surveys of households and legal practitioners and experts, capturing how the rule of law is experienced and perceived. Authoritarian practices have become entrenched In its 2026 global findings, the WJP identified the expansion of authoritarian practices, the narrowing of civic space and the weakening of checks and balances as the principal forces behind the continuing global decline. "Authoritarianism is no longer merely an emerging trend - it has become entrenched in many parts of the world," Alejandro Ponce, the WJP's executive director, said in the report's accompanying statement. The organization said more than 86% of countries and jurisdictions had experienced sustained five-year declines in at least one of three safeguards against authoritarian rule: constraints on government powers, open government or fundamental rights. The latest assessment also found that freedom of opinion and expression declined in 64% of countries, freedom of assembly and association in 67%, and civic participation in 65%. Judicial limits on government power deteriorated in 63% of countries, while civil justice weakened in 64% and criminal justice in 58%. The WJP said undue executive pressure and government interference were major drivers of institutional deterioration in both civil and criminal justice systems. Although these are global findings rather than Ethiopia-specific figures, they provide context for the challenges reflected in Ethiopia's repeated low rankings. The country's performance in constraints on government power, fundamental rights and open government places those concerns at the center of its rule-of-law record. Conflicts and restrictions on civic space form part of the wider context Ethiopia's ranking comes amid continuing insecurity and serious human rights concerns across several regions. Armed conflicts in Amhara, Oromia and parts of Tigray have contributed to a difficult environment for civilian protection, access to justice and the exercise of basic freedoms. Addis Standard has previously reported on extrajudicial killings, torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearances, as well as restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly. A U.S. State Department assessment of Ethiopia's 2024 human rights record, reported by Addis Standard in August 2025, documented abuses attributed to state and non-state actors in the context of ongoing conflicts. The media environment has also remained under pressure. In March 2026, Addis Standard reported on an assessment by International Media Support documenting continued intimidation, detention and harassment of journalists in Ethiopia. The report recorded at least 44 journalists abducted or detained during 2025, compared with 43 in 2024. Such developments are relevant to the rule-of-law assessment because the index considers not only whether laws exist, but also how effectively institutions protect rights, enforce legal safeguards and constrain the exercise of public power. However, the index's aggregate score does not independently establish a direct causal relationship between any single conflict, detention or restriction and Ethiopia's overall ranking. Rather, its indicators provide a broader framework for assessing institutional performance alongside other documented evidence. Regional position underscores Ethiopia's decline Ethiopia's 2025 position of 30th among 34 sub-Saharan African countries placed it near the bottom of the regional table. Its overall score of 0.36 was substantially below those of regional leaders, including Rwanda, Namibia and Mauritius. The regional picture is itself mixed. The WJP has reported broad deterioration across sub-Saharan Africa, although some countries have recorded improvements in particular years. Ethiopia's continued low placement nevertheless points to the difficulty of reversing the institutional weaknesses identified in successive editions. Globally, the 2026 index covers 143 countries and jurisdictions and draws on more than 215,000 household surveys and 3,400 surveys of legal practitioners and experts. It assesses eight dimensions: constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice. Scores range from zero to one, with higher scores indicating stronger adherence to the rule of law. The annual index is designed to measure how people experience the rule of law in practice, rather than simply whether a country has laws, courts or formal constitutional protections with its findings offering a comparative view of the relationship between legal institutions, public accountability and everyday access to justice. This marks a continuation of a multi-year downward trend, with Ethiopia consistently near the bottom in both global and sub-Saharan African comparisons. Press Release October 21, 2026 Updated: October 21, 2026 Ethiopian Americans Urge African Union to Include Amhara People and All Major Stakeholders in Ethiopia’s Peace Process October 21, 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest WhatsApp Linkedin Telegram Viber Congress (SM/file) Washington Update By Mesfin Mekonen Washington, D.C. The Coalition of Ethiopian Americans Civic Organizations has called on the African Union (AU) to ensure that the Amhara people and other major stakeholders are meaningfully included in future peace negotiations aimed at resolving Ethiopia’s ongoing conflicts. In a formal appeal dated October 19, 2026, the coalition urged the AU to pursue a comprehensive, inclusive, and sustainable peace process that addresses the root causes of Ethiopia’s political instability, armed confrontations, and continuing humanitarian crisis. In a letter addressed to His Excellency Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Chairperson of the African Union Commission, the coalition emphasized that lasting peace in Ethiopia cannot be achieved without the meaningful participation of all major stakeholders affected by the country’s conflicts. The letter warned that excluding significant political, ethnic, and religious communities risks undermining the legitimacy and long-term success of peace initiatives. The coalition acknowledged the African Union’s leadership in facilitating the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement between the Ethiopian government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). The agreement was an important step toward ending the devastating war in northern Ethiopia. However, the coalition argued that the limited participation of other major stakeholders highlighted the need for a broader approach to peacebuilding across the country. Although the Pretoria Agreement addressed the conflict between its signatories, Ethiopia continues to face armed confrontations, displacement, insecurity, and serious human rights concerns in several regions. According to the coalition, a peace process that addresses only selected parties cannot resolve the wider political grievances, questions of representation, and security concerns affecting Ethiopia’s diverse population. Amhara Community’s Security and Human Rights Concerns The coalition expressed deep concern over reports of killings, forced displacement, attacks on civilians, and other serious human rights violations affecting the Amhara population. It noted that members of the community have raised longstanding concerns about their security, political representation, and treatment within Ethiopia. The letter also highlighted reports of attacks against Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church clergy, worshippers, and religious institutions. Such incidents, the coalition argued, threaten not only human life and property but also religious freedom, cultural heritage, and the social fabric of Ethiopian society. The coalition called for credible and impartial investigations into allegations of serious human rights violations, effective protection for civilians, and accountability for those responsible under applicable law. It also pointed to ongoing armed confrontations involving government forces and various armed groups, including Fano and factions associated with the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), as evidence of the complexity of Ethiopia’s security crisis. The coalition maintained that military action alone cannot resolve the political grievances and security concerns underlying these conflicts. Instead, it urged the African Union to support meaningful dialogue that addresses the root causes of violence and creates a foundation for peaceful coexistence. Seven Recommendations for Sustainable Peace In its appeal to the African Union Commission, the coalition outlined seven recommendations intended to strengthen the prospects for a comprehensive and lasting peace in Ethiopia. First, ensure the meaningful inclusion of the Amhara people. The coalition urged the AU to ensure that representatives capable of articulating the community’s political, security, and human rights concerns participate directly in peace negotiations. Such participation, it stressed, must be substantive rather than symbolic. Second, broaden participation to include all major stakeholders. The coalition called for an inclusive process involving affected communities, political parties, relevant armed actors, civil society organizations, religious institutions, women’s groups, and other stakeholders. It argued that a credible peace process must reflect Ethiopia’s diversity and recognize the legitimate concerns of communities throughout the country. Third, address the root causes of Ethiopia’s conflicts. The coalition urged negotiators to confront longstanding grievances concerning political representation, equality before the law, security, human rights, constitutional governance, and fundamental freedoms. Without addressing these underlying issues, the coalition warned, any agreement risks producing only a temporary cessation of hostilities rather than a durable settlement. Fourth, strengthen civilian protection and religious freedom. The letter called on all parties to protect civilians, prevent attacks on religious institutions, facilitate humanitarian assistance, and respect international human rights and humanitarian law. It also emphasized the need to protect communities facing violence, displacement, and threats to their religious freedom. Fifth, promote impartial investigations and accountability. The coalition called for credible and independent investigations into reported atrocities and serious human rights violations. It urged the African Union to encourage appropriate investigative mechanisms and accountability measures that apply fairly to all parties, regardless of political affiliation or identity. Sixth, support inclusive national dialogue and democratic reform. The coalition emphasized the need for a credible national dialogue that brings Ethiopia’s diverse communities together to address fundamental political disagreements peacefully. Such a process, it argued, should advance constitutional governance, the rule of law, democratic institutions, minority rights, and equal citizenship. Seventh, establish a comprehensive and sustainable peace framework. The coalition encouraged the African Union to work with the Ethiopian government, relevant political and community representatives, and international partners to develop a framework with clear commitments, mechanisms for monitoring implementation, and meaningful opportunities for affected communities to participate in decisions concerning their future. A Call for Stronger African Union Leadership The coalition stressed that Ethiopia’s continuing instability has consequences beyond its national borders, affecting regional security, humanitarian conditions, and stability throughout the Horn of Africa. As a founding member of the Organization of African Unity, the predecessor of the African Union, Ethiopia has historically played an important role in African diplomacy and continental affairs. The coalition argued that the AU has both a responsibility and an opportunity to help the country move away from armed conflict toward peaceful political coexistence. Achieving that objective, the letter emphasized, will require impartial mediation, broad stakeholder participation, respect for human rights, and a willingness to address the legitimate concerns of all affected communities. “There can be no lasting peace in Ethiopia without the meaningful inclusion of the Amhara population and other major stakeholders in the peace process,” the coalition emphasized in its appeal. The letter warned that excluding important communities risks perpetuating the grievances, political divisions, and security challenges that have contributed to Ethiopia’s recurring conflicts. The coalition therefore urged the African Union Commission to make inclusive participation a central principle of its engagement with Ethiopia and to encourage the establishment of a credible peace process that gives all affected communities a meaningful opportunity to shape their country’s future. International Engagement and Accountability In addition to addressing the African Union, the coalition’s letter was copied to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres, the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Committee. The outreach reflects the coalition’s effort to encourage African and international institutions to support a peace process that prioritizes civilian protection, accountability, national reconciliation, and democratic governance. The coalition stated its readiness to support constructive initiatives promoting peace, respect for human rights, and democratic institutions in Ethiopia. It also expressed hope that, under the leadership of the African Union Commission, a more inclusive and impartial process could help address the concerns of Ethiopia’s diverse communities and establish a foundation for lasting stability. Conclusion: Inclusion Is Essential to Lasting Peace Ethiopia’s path toward peace requires more than agreements between selected parties. It requires a process that recognizes the country’s diverse communities, addresses longstanding grievances, protects fundamental rights, and creates meaningful opportunities for political participation. The central message of the Coalition of Ethiopian Americans Civic Organizations is clear: a sustainable peace agreement must include the Amhara people and all other major stakeholders whose participation is necessary to resolve Ethiopia’s interconnected conflicts. For the African Union, the challenge is to help facilitate a peace process that goes beyond ending individual confrontations and addresses the broader political and security issues threatening the country’s future. An inclusive, impartial, and accountable approach would offer a stronger foundation for national reconciliation and peaceful coexistence. Exclusion, by contrast, risks leaving essential grievances unresolved and prolonging the cycle of conflict. As Ethiopia continues to confront serious challenges, the African Union’s leadership will be important in encouraging dialogue, protecting civilians, and supporting a credible political process. Lasting peace will depend on whether all affected communities have a meaningful voice in shaping Ethiopia’s future. ethiopia.title: The Ethiopia-Djibouti Trade Corridor and the Shared Stakes of Regional Security - horn review
ethiopia.summary: The Ethiopia-Djibouti Trade Corridor is crucial for both nations, with over 95% of Ethiopia's trade relying on this route, which also significantly supports Djibouti's economy. Recent tensions, particularly the TPLF-Shabiya's attempts to disrupt this corridor, pose risks not only to Ethiopia's economic stability but also to Djibouti's port revenues. The Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) has shown military superiority, yet threats to the corridor highlight vulnerabilities that could be exploited by opposing forces. The situation underscores the need for enhanced bilateral security cooperation and integrated defense strategies to protect this vital infrastructure. Recent military developments, including the ENDF's counteroffensive, have temporarily reversed rebel advances, but ongoing vigilance and coordinated efforts are essential to ensure the corridor's security and maintain regional stability.

Now, forecasters warn that El Niño flooding in the coming months could push the country’s hardest-hit communities toward famine. Be part of what makes CARE possible. Somalia has two rainy seasons. The second, called the Deyr, usually runs from October to December. Recent forecasts project that the 2026-2027 El Niño season may make the Deyr far more severe, bringing heavy rain and flooding before the end of the year. For families who have spent years watching crops wither and livestock die, more water might sound like relief. It is not. Deyr rain can become torrential, triggering flash floods and causing rivers to overflow. During the 2023 El Niño floods, 1.2 million people were displaced across Somalia. This year, Somalia’s disaster authorities estimate that 2.5 million to 3.5 million people could be exposed to flooding, with as many as 1 million at risk of further displacement. In 2023, forecasts allowed the Somali government, World Food Programme (WFP), and other partners to send early warnings , distribute cash before flooding began, and pre-position supplies in high-risk areas. Similar preparations are underway this year , but much of the network that made that possible no longer exists. The people in the path of the flooding have already lost nearly everything. Years of failed rains killed their livestock and destroyed their harvests, driving many into displacement settlements that sit on low ground near the rivers. Some communities hit by the 2023 floods are still living with destroyed homes, damaged irrigation systems, and lost herds three years later. How flooding makes hunger worse Mother Aisha feeds her 1-year-old daughter Shukri at a CARE-supported health center near Dhahar, Somalia. The health center was forced to close at the end of September 2026. Photo: Sarah Easter/CARE What is the IPC? The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) is the system governments, UN agencies, and aid organizations use to measure hunger on a common scale. Analysts review data on food consumption, malnutrition, and deaths, then agree on a classification for each situation and area. The scale has five phases: Minimal, Stressed, Crisis, Emergency, and Catastrophe/Famine. What do emergency, catastrophe, and famine mean? IPC Phase 4, Emergency: Families face large food gaps or can only meet basic food needs by selling essential assets, taking on debt, or exhausting other resources they need to survive. Acute malnutrition is very high, and the risk of death increases. IPC Phase 5, Catastrophe: Individual households face an extreme lack of food even after exhausting those coping strategies. Starvation, destitution, extremely critical acute malnutrition, and increased deaths can occur. IPC Phase 5, Famine: Famine is an area-wide classification. It is reached only when extreme hunger is widespread and specific thresholds for acute malnutrition and deaths are also met. That means households can already be living in Catastrophe before the wider area is formally classified as being in famine. Floodwaters do more than destroy homes. They can wipe out crops and livestock, cut off roads to markets and health facilities, eliminate other sources of income, and force families to leave their homes in search of safety, income, and stability. For people who are eating too little, these losses can quickly deepen hunger. Between October and December, 5.4 million people are projected to face Crisis levels of hunger or worse. Nearly 1.5 million are expected to reach Emergency, when families face severe food shortages or must exhaust the assets they rely on to survive. Around 26,000 displaced people in Baidoa are projected to reach Catastrophe, the highest household classification on the IPC scale. At that point, families still cannot meet their basic food needs even after exhausting extreme ways of coping. People can face starvation, destitution, extremely critical levels of acute malnutrition, and a sharply increased risk of death. The IPC warns that under a plausible worst-case scenario involving more severe flooding and displacement, displaced communities could face a risk of famine by the end of 2026. Hunger, disease, and fewer services to respond Fadumo, 42, fled violence in Somalia’s Hiiraan region and now lives with her children in a displacement camp outside Mogadishu. Photo: Sarah Easter/CARE Flooding also brings another danger to people who are already malnourished: disease. Floodwaters can contaminate drinking water, damage toilets and sanitation systems, and increase the risk of diarrhea and other waterborne illnesses. Somalia is already contending with disease outbreaks, including cholera, measles , and diphtheria . For young children, malnutrition and illness can reinforce each other. Malnutrition weakens the body’s ability to fight infection, while illnesses such as diarrhea can make it harder to absorb nutrients, increasing the risk of dehydration. A child who is already experiencing hunger can become much sicker, much faster. Nearly 1.92 million children under five are expected to require treatment for acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027, including 433,000 with severe acute malnutrition. But the services designed to interrupt that cycle are shrinking. Somalia’s humanitarian response relies heavily on funding from governments and other international donors. Since early 2025, humanitarian funding has fallen sharply as major government donors have reduced foreign assistance, with cuts in U.S. funding accounting for a significant part of the decline. This has forced the closure of many health, nutrition, food, water, and cash programs. In one displacement camp outside Mogadishu, those losses have happened all at once. Since May, health services, water distribution, food assistance, emergency cash, and safe spaces for women and girls have stopped. Fadumo, a 42-year-old mother living there with her extended family, says they now plan only “day by day, hour by hour.” When money comes in, she says, the most urgent need is always food. Across Somalia, more than 230 nutrition centers have closed , and an estimated 1.1 million women and children are expected to lose access to treatment and preventative nutrition services. Of the 75 CARE- and partner-supported facilities that have been treating acute malnutrition in the country, only six are expected to remain operational after September. Admissions to stabilization centers for children with severe acute malnutrition have already risen by 40%. “We are being forced to close lifesaving health centers not because the need has disappeared, but because the funding has,” says CARE Somalia country director Ummy Dubow. “If these facilities shut their doors just as the rains arrive, the consequences will be measured in children’s lives.” The window to prevent famine closes when the roads do Women farmers, members of women's groups in East Darfur, receive improved seeds and agricultural tools on a cart in Abu Karinka, East Darfur. The supplies will be used for their vegetable farm. Photo: CARE Early forecasts give Somalia time to act before the worst flooding begins. The government and humanitarian organizations, including CARE, are using forecasts to identify high-risk communities, issue warnings, prepare evacuation plans, and position assistance before roads become inaccessible. CARE is working with local partners, authorities, and communities to provide cash assistance, healthcare, nutrition support, and protection services, including support for women and girls, where funding allows. But early warnings only work if communities have the resources to respond. CARE is calling for increased, flexible humanitarian funding, greater support for local and women-led organizations, and safe humanitarian access so food, medicine, clean water, cash, and other assistance can reach people before and during flooding. Timing matters, too. Once floodwaters cut off roads and transportation routes, reaching displaced communities, delivering food and medicine, or helping people move to safety becomes much harder. Families can also lose access to markets, health facilities, clean water, and other essential services just when they need them most. Somalia saw the value of acting early in 2023, when forecasts triggered cash assistance and warnings before floodwaters arrived. The goal now is not to wait for famine to be declared, but to prevent communities from reaching that point. CARE has been working in Somalia since 1981 . Our main program activities since then have included projects in water and sanitation, sustainable pastoralist activities, civil society and media development, small-scale enterprise development, primary school education, teacher training, adult literacy, and vocational training. We work in partnership with Somali and international aid agencies, civil society leaders, and local authorities. Most recently, CARE has broadened its work to include economic empowerment, food and nutrition security, humanitarian response, and reproductive health. somalia.summary: After enduring years of drought, Somalia faces a new crisis as forecasts predict severe flooding due to the El Niño phenomenon, potentially pushing vulnerable communities toward famine. The country narrowly avoided famine during its last major drought, but many essential health and nutrition programs have since closed due to funding shortages. With the Deyr rainy season approaching, which typically runs from October to December, experts warn that heavy rains could lead to flash floods, displacing millions and exacerbating food insecurity. Currently, 5.4 million people are projected to experience Crisis levels of hunger, with nearly 1.5 million facing Emergency conditions. The situation is further complicated by the risk of disease outbreaks linked to flooding, which can contaminate water supplies and worsen malnutrition. Humanitarian organizations, including CARE, are urging for increased funding and support to prepare for the impending floods and prevent famine, emphasizing the need for timely intervention to save lives and stabilize affected communities.

somalia.title: Why Ilhan Omar’s case gives US Somalis a bad name - アラブニュース
somalia.content: Why Ilhan Omar’s case gives US Somalis a bad name ARAB NEWS ARAB NEWS GLOBAL ARAB NEWS PK ARAB NEWS FR 22 Oct 2026 Since 1975 SEARCH 検索: × JP ARAB NEWS JP SEARCH 検索: Japan Saudi Arabia Middle East Business Features Arts & Culture × Japan Saudi Arabia Middle East Business Features Arts & Culture JP Home Middle East Why Ilhan Omar’s case gives US Somalis a bad name Why Ilhan Omar’s case gives US Somalis a bad name Short Url: 22 Oct 2026 15:49:27 GMT9 22 Oct 2026 15:49:27 GMT9 Share Accused of immigration fraud and false statements in citizenship documents, the Minnesota congresswoman can face revoking citizenship and deportation Ray Hanania CHICAGO: A federal investigation into how Ilhan Omar, a member of Congress from Minnesota, obtained US citizenship has raised questions about whether she, or her late father, misrepresented her age on immigration documents. If proven, the allegations could expose her to criminal charges, denaturalization and possible deportation. Federal agents searched her Washington home on Oct. 12, just weeks before the midterm elections on Nov. 3, and seized her phone, computers, passport and other documents. The Justice Department has described the search as part of an ongoing criminal investigation but Omar, the US representative for Minnesota’s 5th congressional district since 2019, has not been charged and the government has not publicly disclosed all of its evidence. The focus of the probe is reportedly on whether she or her late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, misstated her age on immigration documents. Investigators are examining whether her age was listed as 17, rather than 18, when her father became a US citizen in 2000. This is a key distinction because at the time, minors age 17 or under could be granted citizenship automatically through a parent. Adults, age 18 and over, had to submit an application of their own. Her father’s past in Somalia is also reportedly under scrutiny. Mohamed, a former cab driver and postal worker, died in 2020 from COVID-19 complications. A New York Post report alleged that he “misrepresented himself as a refugee” despite a decades-long military career, including a leadership position under Somali dictator Siad Barre — a claim that, if verified, could have affected his application. The probe also touches on long-running, but unproven, allegations that Omar entered the country illegally, and claims that her previous marriage to Ahmed Nur Said Elmi was arranged to help him obtain immigration benefits, including the suggestion that he is actually her brother. Omar has repeatedly denied the accusations and none of the marriage-related allegations have been established in court. She also faces a separate inquiry into financial disclosures. This centers on two businesses linked to her husband, Tim Mynett, that appeared to leap in value in her 2025 filing. She amended the filings in April this year to greatly reduce the valuations, and her office said the original figures were mistakes that did not properly account for liabilities and ownership. In September, a congressional ethics watchdog recommended clearing her of any wrongdoing, according to reports. CNN described the search of her home this month as “unusually aggressive,” and said it targeted possible false statements on government documents and a potential conspiracy. Before signing off on it, US Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh limited how prosecutors could access materials seized from a sitting lawmaker. The restrictions were intended to protect Omar’s legislative activities, which are shielded from scrutiny by federal prosecutors under the Constitution’s “speech or debate” clause. Omar’s attorneys said those safeguards were not followed. In a letter to the Department of Justice, they said agents violated “key restrictions” attached to the warrant, failed to promptly provide her legal team with a copy of the warrant, and did not contact the House of Representatives’ Office of General Counsel before the search, as required. Citing people familiar with the situation, Politico reported on Tuesday that investigators had not yet accessed Omar’s phone. If they attempt to do so, they must first give her a chance to assert protections on speech or debate, and a court would decide what investigators are allowed to see. Since the raid, investigators have also turned their attention toward Omar’s relatives. Fox News reported on Monday that her sister, author and activist Sahra Noor, “voluntarily” spoke with investigators about Omar’s immigration status. Officials have not confirmed who else was subpoenaed, and Noor did not respond to a request for comment. The evidence made public so far does not establish that Omar knowingly misrepresented information to obtain US citizenship. The Department of Justice has not publicly presented evidence that she knowingly falsified immigration or citizenship documents, and no court has found her guilty of immigration fraud. The DoJ declined to comment when contacted by Arab News. “As a general rule, the department declines to comment on ongoing investigations,” a spokesperson said on Tuesday. Omar previously declined to speak with Arab News and did not respond to another request for comment sent through her campaign website. US law allows the government to seek the revocation of a naturalized citizen’s citizenship if it was obtained illegally, or secured through the concealment of a material fact or willful misrepresentation. To denaturalize Omar, the DoJ would have to bring a civil lawsuit in federal court and prove that she or her father willfully misrepresented a material fact, such as her age, in order to obtain citizenship. If prosecutors brought criminal charges, they could potentially include immigration fraud, false statements on government forms, or conspiracy, depending on the evidence. Any case based solely on statements made during the original naturalization process could face significant time-limit issues, given that Omar became a citizen more than two decades ago. Investigators were reportedly examining whether similar information appeared on later documents, such as passport applications, which could raise separate questions about more recent conduct. If the government successfully revoked Omar’s citizenship, she could face deportation proceedings. Legal experts told CNN that denaturalization was a “relatively rare process” and prosecutors would have to show that any misleading statements were intentional. Between 2008 and June 12, 2026, 166 denaturalization complaints were filed, according to data gathering and research organization the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse. This represents an annual average of fewer than 10 cases, and a minuscule fraction of the hundreds of thousands of people who become naturalized American citizens each year. The investigation has also raised concerns about a possible backlash against the Somali-American community. Jaylani Hussein, executive director of the Minnesota chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, described the rhetoric surrounding Omar and the wider Somali community as “Islamophobic, racist, and xenophobic.” In the past, some conservative commentators in Muslim American and Somali American circles have criticized Omar’s progressive positions as inconsistent with the socially conservative and deeply religious values held by many within those communities. In an op-ed published by the Wall Street Journal in 2019, Somali-born author Ayaan Hirsi Ali compared her own experiences with those of Omar, and accused the politician of failing to confront antisemitism within Muslim communities. Omar has rejected the allegations and accused federal authorities of targeting her for political reasons. Her lawyers described the search this month as “vindictive, retributive and politically motivated.” Omar has sought to turn the investigation into a rallying call. In a video posted on Tuesday, she thanked supporters who had sent “$5, $10, $20” and said the contributions would help her fight the administration in Washington. She said the coming period would be “very expensive and challenging” and urged supporters to continue donating. Previously, she vowed that she and her allies would not be “intimidated” or “silenced.” Share Related Articles Trump behind bars... in Tehran propaganda installation Could Lebanon be dragged into another war if Israel-Iran tensions explode? somalia.content: Aid cuts threaten devastating toll in Somalia, ICRC warns - World - Chinadaily.com.cn Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER MOBILE Global Edition ASIA 中文 双语 Français HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS CULTURE TRAVEL VIDEO SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL NEWSPAPER China Daily PDF China Daily E-paper MOBILE World Asia-Pacific Americas Europe Middle East Africa China-US China-Europe China-Japan China-Africa Home World / Africa Home / World / Africa Aid cuts threaten devastating toll in Somalia, ICRC warns By VICTOR RABALLA in Nairobi, Kenya | chinadaily.com.cn | Updated: 2026-10-22 21:27 Share Share - WeChat CLOSE A sharp decline in humanitarian funding could have devastating consequences for vulnerable communities in Somalia as looming floods compound the effects of drought and conflict. The head of the International Committee of the Red Cross in the country has warned that the beginning of the El Nino in some parts of the country risks deaths and property damage if urgent measures are not taken. Antoine Grand made an appeal to international donors to sustain assistance to the Horn of Africa nation, saying the closure of nutrition centers and health facilities was leaving families with fewer places to turn as successive crises exhausted their ability to recover. "We know there are other priorities in the world today, but don't forget about Somalia," Grand said. He estimated that humanitarian funding for Somalia had fallen from about $2.3 billion in 2022 to roughly $300-$350 million, leaving a response already focused on the most urgent needs severely underfunded. Aid organizations had prioritized essential, lifesaving activities, yet the United Nations humanitarian appeal was only about 30 percent funded, he said. "When you reduce that aid drastically, then it is brutal and people suffer," Grand said. The UN and its partners launched an $852 million appeal in January to assist 2.4 million people in Somalia this year. Grand said funding shortages across the humanitarian sector had forced nutrition centers to close, reduced support for hospitals and halted water and resilience projects. "At clinics supported by the ICRC and the Somali Red Crescent Society, patient numbers had nearly doubled as surrounding facilities closed," he said. The impact was especially severe for malnourished children, as access to treatment continue to dwindle. Somalia's vulnerability stems from the combination of prolonged conflict, repeated climate shocks and weak public services, he said. Around 3.3 million people are displaced, with many living in settlements where access to clean water, sanitation and healthcare is limited. Families that lose livestock or crops during drought have little opportunity to rebuild before another emergency strikes. "More and more Somali families are really on the brink of just collapsing," Grand said. He said the impending floods could deepen losses, particularly along the Shabelle and Juba rivers. In a warning issued last week, the ICRC said anticipated El Nino conditions could intensify the October-December rains, threatening farmland and displacement settlements. Grand described the dilemma facing farmers near Jowhar, where planting risks losing scarce seeds to floodwaters, while leaving fields idle would deepen food insecurity and hunger. He said early warnings are helping families move before flooding, giving them time to take livestock, household belongings and important documents. ICRC and Somali Red Crescent have stocked supported health facilities with additional medicines, positioned emergency supplies near vulnerable communities and prepared boats for rescue operations and aid deliveries. "Teams have also protected 38 strategic water points to reduce the risk of floodwater contamination and waterborne disease," Grand added. Beyond emergency assistance, he called for sustained investment in reliable water systems, roads, drainage and flood protection to help communities withstand future shocks. "Anticipatory action, preparedness, resilience is extremely important. We need to invest in that. The more we invest in preparing for the next crisis, the less impact will this next crisis have," Grand said.
