somalia.content: Somali Media Officials Begin 21-Day AI and Counter-Disinformation Training in China - Somali News today Live Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Home Politics Security Elections More News Premium Economy & Business Education Entertainment & Lifestyle Environment & Climate Health International Relations Technology & Innovation Sports News By Region Nationwide Benadir Galmudug Hirshabelle Jubaland Puntland South West State Somaliland North Eastern State Resources Infographics Downloads Videos FAQ About Somalia Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Generic selectors Exact matches only Search in title Search in content Post Type Selectors Technology & Innovation Nationwide Somali Media Officials Begin 21-Day AI and Counter-Disinformation Training in China October 22, 2026 5 min read JINHUA , A 21-day training programme for 27 officials from Somalia’s Ministry of Information, Culture and Tourism has opened in Jinhua, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, focusing on modern media strategies, artificial intelligence, and combating misinformation. The programme, delivered by experts from Zhejiang Normal University, brings together directors, heads of government media departments, and other ministry personnel. Participants will study modern media strategies, the application of AI in communication, media management, and techniques for identifying and countering false information. The initiative is part of broader efforts to strengthen the professional skills of Somali government media staff as the country seeks to modernise its public communication systems and adapt to changes in the digital media landscape. A Relationship Built Over Months of Engagement The training did not emerge in isolation. It follows a series of high-level engagements between Mogadishu and Beijing on media and technology cooperation throughout 2026. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Somalia’s AI integration , the Ministry of Information has already implemented advanced AI systems in national media operations, including automated translation, content generation, and digital distribution algorithms that have reduced editorial production time. In August 2026, Information Minister Abdulfatah Kasim Mohamud met with Cao Shumin, Minister of China’s National Radio and Television Administration, in Beijing to discuss media modernisation, institutional capacity building, and professional training. The Minister also participated in the China-Africa Media Cooperation Forum, where he called for stronger support to modernise Somali broadcasting infrastructure, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Somalia’s engagement with Chinese and Arab media institutions . At the opening ceremony in Jinhua, Zhu Yifeng, Vice-President of Zhejiang Normal University, said the workshop would promote the exchange of media expertise, strengthen bilateral ties, and advance cooperation between Somalia and China. Abdishakur Ali Ahmed, Director of the Media Strategy Department at Somalia’s Ministry of Information, said the training offered government media representatives an opportunity to learn from China’s experience in modernising its media sector. He thanked the Chinese government, organisers, and institutions involved, particularly the Chinese Ministry of Commerce, which financed the training, and the Chinese Embassy in Somalia, led by Ambassador Wang Yu, which facilitated the initiative. The Strategic Logic and Its Limits China’s engagement with Somali media is part of a broader pattern of Beijing’s involvement in Africa’s information and communication sectors, alongside its expanding economic and security ties with Mogadishu. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of China’s trade policy , Beijing has extended zero-tariff access to all 53 African nations, and the two countries have deepened defence and security cooperation. The media training represents another dimension of a relationship that now spans trade, security, and information. For Somalia, the appeal is practical. The country’s state media infrastructure remains weak, despite recent investments. In 2025, the Ministry of Information established Somalia’s first Media Satellite Teleport in over three decades, a facility intended to modernise broadcasting capabilities, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the teleport launch . But infrastructure alone is insufficient. The government has struggled to counter Al-Shabaab ’s sophisticated propaganda operations and to manage the rapid spread of misinformation during political crises. The challenges facing Somali media are not limited to technical capacity. As reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of media freedom concerns , independent outlets have accused the government of orchestrating digital censorship campaigns, including copyright strikes and bot-driven harassment against critical reporting. Journalists have been arrested and assaulted by security forces, with press freedom organizations documenting a pattern of intimidation. Critical Note The Jinhua training programme is a welcome investment in Somali media capacity, and the focus on artificial intelligence and counter-disinformation addresses genuine gaps in the government’s communication apparatus. The involvement of the Chinese Ministry of Commerce as a financier and the embassy in Mogadishu as a facilitator indicates a level of institutional commitment that suggests this is not a one-off gesture. But the programme also raises questions that its organisers have not addressed. AI tools and modern media strategies are only as effective as the institutions that deploy them. Somalia’s Ministry of Information has struggled with limited budgets, political interference, and a state media apparatus that many Somalis view with skepticism. A 21-day training course can introduce new techniques, but it cannot resolve these structural weaknesses. The deeper concern is one of orientation. China’s model of media management involves tight state control over information flows, a framework that is fundamentally different from the pluralistic, if chaotic, media environment that has emerged in Mogadishu over the past decade. The training is framed as technical, but the techniques being transferred are not politically neutral. How Somalia’s government media officials apply what they learn in Jinhua will depend on the political culture they return to. The programme can teach them how to use AI to detect misinformation. It cannot teach them how to resist the temptation to use the same tools for political advantage. The same ministry that is sending officials to learn about countering disinformation is the one accused of orchestrating digital censorship at home . Local media reports said two members of Laftagaren’s forces were killed when their motorcycle was struck. Abdulkadir and Mustafa Qoomaal, a military figure affiliated with the forces, survived unscathed. It remains unclear whether the strike was intended to assassinate Abdulkadir, who is believed to be the principal strategist behind the guerrilla campaign waged by Laftagaren’s forces since the former regional president was ousted in a federal government offensive in March. General Ahmed visited Italy’s Training and Doctrine Command headquarters in Turin, the Italian Special Forces School, and other training and educational facilities under the Italian command. He held meetings with his Italian counterparts to discuss strengthening cooperation in training, improving the knowledge and skills of Somali forces, and expanding Italy’s support for the Somali National Army. The visit is the latest in a series of high-level engagements between Somali and Italian defense officials in 2026. In July, the Commander of Somalia’s Special Forces, Adam Mohamed Omar, met with the Commander of the Italian Special Operations Command, Admiral Paolo Pezzutti, in Rome to discuss advanced training and capacity building for Somali special operations units. In May, Somali Infantry Commander General Sahal Abdullahi Omar hosted an Italian military delegation in Mogadishu to discuss tactical support and training for ground troops, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the earlier defense talks . Italy’s Deepening Role in Somalia’s Security Sector Italy has been one of Somalia’s most consistent security partners, both bilaterally and through the European Union. In September 2026, Defence Minister Ahmed Moallim Fiqi met with a senior Italian delegation led by General Giovanni Maria Iannucci, Commander of Italy’s Joint Operations Command, to discuss expanding security and defense cooperation, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the meeting . General Iannucci’s visit to Mogadishu was part of a broader regional mission that also included Djibouti and Saudi Arabia, with Italian officials emphasizing that Red Sea security directly affects Italy’s national interests. Italy is the largest contributor to the EU Training Mission in Somalia (EUTM Somalia), with approximately 150 military personnel deployed. The mission, which has operated since 2010, provides training, mentoring, and advisory support to Somali defense institutions. In October 2026, Italian Brigadier General Ivan Falasca took command of EUTM Somalia, succeeding Brigadier General Elio Manes. Beyond EUTM, Italy leads the Bilateral Training Mission for Somali and Djiboutian Police Forces (MIADIT Somalia), implemented by the Carabinieri. The mission, which resumed activities in September 2026, focuses on building the capacity of Somali police forces in security and territorial control. Italy’s engagement has also extended to formal agreements. In July 2026, Somali Internal Security Minister Abdullahi Sheikh Ismail (Fartaag) and Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi signed a Memorandum of Understanding on police development, counter-terrorism, and border management, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the agreement . The Strategic Context Italy’s defense engagement in Somalia is driven by both historical ties and contemporary strategic interests. The stability of the Horn of Africa and the safety of navigation in the Red Sea directly impact Italy’s security and economic interests. General Iannucci stated during his September visit that “defending free navigation here is equivalent to defending Italy.” The training relationship has also extended to specialized units. Italy’s Col Moschin special forces regiment has previously trained Somali bodyguard units in Livorno, and Italian officials have discussed establishing a national military training and advisory mission in Mogadishu. The Somali Army Chief, Brigadier General Ibrahim Mohamed Mahmoud, met with Italy’s Defense Attaché, Captain Antonino Mazzocca, in February 2026, with Italy reaffirming its commitment to training and equipment support, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the meeting . Critical Note Italy’s commitment to Somali military training is substantial and sustained, and the frequency of high-level consultations reflects a genuine partnership. The Italian model, combining bilateral training, EU mission leadership, and police capacity-building through the Carabinieri, is more comprehensive than that of most other partners. But the visit also highlights a persistent question: how much of this training translates into lasting operational capability. Italy has trained Somali forces for over a decade through EUTM, yet the Somali National Army remains dependent on external support for logistics, pay, and specialized capabilities. The Training and Doctrine Command, which General Ahmed heads, is the institution responsible for converting foreign training into a self-sustaining system. Its ability to do so depends on resources and institutional stability that the Somali government has struggled to provide. Italy’s engagement also carries a geopolitical dimension. As Rome deepens its role alongside Türkiye, Egypt, and other partners, the coordination among these external actors becomes critical. Fragmented training programmes with different doctrines and standards can create parallel systems rather than a unified force. The challenge for Somalia is to manage these partnerships in a way that builds a coherent national army, not a patchwork of externally trained units. General Ahmed’s visit to Turin is a step in that direction. Whether it produces results will depend on what happens after the delegation returns to Mogadishu. According to a statement released by NIRA, the Hubiye platform enables financial institutions, telecommunications companies, and government agencies to verify an individual’s identity against the national database before processing transactions or granting access to services. The system is intended to reduce identity fraud while facilitating smoother interactions between citizens and the institutions that serve them. How the Verification Works The Hubiye platform operates by linking a citizen’s Unique Identification Number with authorized relying parties. When a bank, telecom operator, or government office needs to confirm an identity, the system performs a dual-layer check: it validates the ID against NIRA’s central database and then confirms the individual’s presence through a real-time One-Time Password sent to the citizen’s registered device. This structure is designed to prevent a common vulnerability in identity systems, where a stolen or forged card can be presented without the holder’s knowledge. The OTP requirement ensures that verification requires the active participation of the ID holder, adding a layer of security that a physical card alone cannot provide. NIRA has described the platform as the foundation of Somalia’s identification ecosystem, with the capacity to support verification for citizens residing abroad as well, through integration with international agencies. The Broader Push for Digital Identity Hubiye is one component of a larger digital infrastructure that NIRA has been building since the passage of the Identification and Registration Act in March 2023. The authority has registered more than 1.5 million Somalis with biometric digital identities, processing between 12,000 and 15,000 registrations daily, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the national ID rollout . The government’s target is to reach 15 million citizens by 2029. The National ID has already become mandatory for domestic air travel, passport applications, and opening a bank account. The Auditor General’s Office is integrating the government payroll system with NIRA’s database to eliminate ghost workers, with completion targeted for December 2027. NIRA has also launched the eAqoonsi mobile application, allowing citizens to carry their National ID digitally on smartphones with the same legal validity as the physical card, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the digital ID app . Critical Note The launch of Hubiye represents a meaningful technical advance. A national ID system is only as valuable as its verification mechanisms, and the OTP layer addresses a real weakness in card-based identity systems. For banks and telecom companies operating in Somalia, a reliable, real-time verification tool reduces the risk of fraud and simplifies customer onboarding, both of which are prerequisites for financial inclusion and investment. But the platform’s effectiveness will be tested by the same constraints that have challenged NIRA’s broader rollout. The agency does not officially operate in Puntland, Somaliland, or Jubbaland, where political and administrative obstacles have prevented registration. Puntland has established its own identification authority and rejected the federal system. A verification platform that covers only part of the country’s population and territory cannot function as a national identity infrastructure. It can only serve the regions where NIRA is operational. The data security procedures that NIRA has implemented are a welcome signal that the authority recognizes the sensitivity of the information it holds. The National Data Protection Act and the establishment of a Data Protection Authority provide a legal framework. Whether those safeguards are sufficient, and whether they are enforced consistently, will determine whether Somalis trust the system enough to use it. The Hubiye platform is a tool for verification. It is not, by itself, a guarantee of trust. According to a statement from the Somali National News Agency (SONNA), the meeting focused on strengthening the long-standing friendship between Somalia and Japan and exploring avenues for broader collaboration in areas of mutual interest, including peace, stability, and development. A Partnership Spanning Security, Livelihoods, and Governance Japan’s engagement in Somalia extends well beyond diplomatic courtesy. In May 2026, Japan funded a police instructor training program at the General Kaahiye Police Training School in Mogadishu, implemented in partnership with the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM). Tokyo has also donated equipment to the Somali Police Force’s Mine Action Unit and supported training for female officers in explosive ordnance disposal, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of Japan’s security sector support . On the economic front, Japan has been a significant contributor to Somalia’s blue economy ambitions. In late 2025, Japan, Somalia, and the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization launched a two-year, $2 million project to revitalize the fisheries sector, focusing on sustainable management, job creation, and food security. The agreement was signed by Ambassador Hiroshi Matsuura and FAO Somalia Representative Etienne Peterschmitt, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the fisheries partnership . The initiative aimed to modernize fish processing and storage facilities, train local fishermen in sustainable practices, and enhance value chains for coastal communities. A subsequent launch ceremony in December 2025, attended by Deputy Minister of Fisheries Ali Ifiye Ali, underscored the project’s focus on combating illegal fishing and strengthening marine resource management, as detailed in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the fisheries modernization launch . Japan has also supported Somali women and girls through the LEAP project, implemented by UN Women, which reached more than 440 women with leadership training, protection services, and livelihood opportunities. The program, funded by Tokyo, has helped women transition from reliance on aid to running small businesses and leading local protection committees, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the LEAP initiative . Debt Relief and Diplomatic Expansion Japan’s relationship with Somalia has also been shaped by debt relief and diplomatic engagement. In November 2024, Somalia’s Finance Minister Bihi Egeh and Japan’s Deputy Head of Mission Ogihara Hiroshi signed an agreement finalizing Somalia’s debt relief process, building on the Paris Club accord that canceled much of the country’s debt, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the debt relief agreement . Diplomatically, Somalia has sought to expand its footprint in East Asia. In August 2025, Somalia’s Ambassador to China, Dr. Hodan Osman, presented her credentials to Japan as a non-resident ambassador, a move officials described as a milestone in broadening partnerships with one of the world’s largest economies, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the accreditation . Critical Note Tuesday’s meeting between Minister Abdisalam and Ambassador Hiroshi is a routine diplomatic engagement, but it reflects a relationship that has quietly become one of Somalia’s more substantive partnerships in Asia. Japan’s contributions span security training, fisheries development, women’s empowerment, and debt relief, a breadth that few other bilateral partners can match. What is notable about Japan’s approach is its emphasis on implementation through multilateral channels. The fisheries project is implemented with the FAO. The police training is conducted with AUSSOM. The women’s empowerment program runs through UN Women. This model allows Japan to contribute to Somalia’s development while minimizing its direct footprint and security exposure, a pragmatic approach for a country whose constitution limits overseas military engagement. The challenge, as with all donor partnerships in Somalia, is sustainability. The fisheries project is a two-year initiative. The police training is a discrete program. The LEAP project reaches hundreds of women, not thousands. These are meaningful interventions, but they are not transformative at scale. Japan’s value to Somalia lies less in the volume of its assistance than in the reliability of its engagement and the technical quality of its support. Whether that support expands or remains at its current level will depend on factors beyond Mogadishu’s control, including Japan’s own budgetary priorities and the trajectory of Somalia’s political stability.
